title: Suicidal Ideation — What the Body Shows

safetyGate.resourceBody:
It covers the warning signs, how to ask someone whether they are thinking about suicide, and how to help them. It contains no details of methods.

If you are thinking about suicide yourself, or you are worried about someone right now, please contact one of the lines above before you read on. They are free and confidential, and they welcome calls from people who are worried about someone else.

regions.org: Numéro national de prévention du suicide
Find A Helpline: free lines in over 130 countries

hook: The body can show that someone is struggling, but not whether they are thinking about suicide; only asking can tell you, and asking is safe.
why:
More than seven hundred thousand people die by suicide each year, about one death in every hundred worldwide, and in most countries the majority are men. Behind each death are families, friends and colleagues, many of whom later wonder what they missed. This chapter answers that question honestly. The body can show you that someone is struggling, sometimes clearly, as earlier chapters in this part described. It cannot show you whether a person is thinking about suicide. No posture, face or gesture tells you that, and decades of research have not found one that does.

What the body gives you is a reason to ask. This chapter teaches the warning signs worth knowing, why men are at particular risk, how to ask the question directly and why asking is safe, what to do in the minutes after someone says yes, how time, distance and a written plan help a crisis pass, and why staying in touch afterwards matters. It ends with looking after yourself, because helping someone through this is heavy. If you are struggling as you read, the resources at the start of this chapter are for you too, and they are open now.

teach.h: The body shows struggle, not suicide.
teach.p:
Everything in this part of the book has been about reading distress: the stooped posture and slowed movement of low mood, the braced shoulders of stress, the mask of “I'm fine”, the heavier drinking, the withdrawal and the exhaustion. These are worth noticing, and people who are thinking about suicide often show some of them. But most people who show them are not thinking about suicide, and some people who are thinking about it show none of them, or hide them well.

The research is humbling. In 2017, Joseph Franklin and colleagues pooled fifty years of studies of risk factors for suicidal thoughts and behaviour, 365 studies in all. Across every kind of risk factor they examined, including depression, hopelessness and previous attempts, prediction was only slightly better than chance, and it had not improved over the decades. The authors did not say that risk factors are useless; they said that, on their own, they cannot tell you who will act. If the best-studied risk factors cannot do that, a reading of someone's posture across a room certainly cannot.

This has a clear practical consequence. Do not wait until someone's body looks bad enough. Do not reassure yourself because a friend still goes to work, still laughs, still turns up. And do not use reading as a substitute for the conversation. The body's job in this chapter is to raise a question, never to answer it.

The figure here sits folded and closed. You might see this shape in someone you love after a loss, or after a long hard stretch. It tells you that something is heavy. It does not tell you what, or how heavy. Only the person can tell you that, and only if someone asks.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if research found a visible signal that reliably separates people who are thinking about suicide from people who are struggling in other ways. Fifty years of risk-factor research, pooled by Franklin and colleagues, has not found one.
teach.pullQuote: The body can tell you someone is struggling. Only a question can tell you whether they are thinking about suicide.

teach.h: Warning signs live in words, changes and goodbyes.
teach.p:
Risk factors describe who is at higher risk over years. Warning signs describe what may be happening now. In 2006, a working group of the American Association of Suicidology, led by David Rudd, set out a consensus list of warning signs for the public, and crisis services publish similar lists today. The clearest signs are things people say: talking about wanting to die, about having no reason to live, about feeling trapped or in unbearable pain, or about being a burden to others. Treat these as serious every time, including when they are said as a joke or in passing.

The next signs are changes in behaviour: drinking or using drugs more, withdrawing from friends and activities, sleeping far more or far less, acting anxious, agitated or reckless, showing rage or talking about revenge, and large swings in mood. Some people say goodbye as though for the last time, give away things that matter to them, or suddenly put their affairs in order. Some lists also include a sudden calm after a long period of distress. That calm can mean many things, including real relief, and the evidence for it as a sign is thin; treat it, like the rest, as a reason to check in.

Much of this list overlaps with the body. Withdrawal shows in where a person sits and how soon they leave. Agitation shows in restless hands and pacing. Neglect shows in clothes and grooming. But notice that the strongest signs are words, which is why listening matters as much as looking, and why a comment that makes the room go quiet deserves a private follow-up rather than a change of subject.

Even the people who wrote these lists call them prompts, not tests. Lanny Berman, then the association's executive director, conceded that their accuracy was “not great”. Their purpose is to get you to ask, and to get the person to help.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if warning signs predicted suicide accurately enough to be used as a test. Their own authors present them as prompts to ask and to seek help, and concede that their accuracy is limited.

teach.p:
Men die by suicide at higher rates than women in most countries. The World Health Organization's estimates for 2019 put the global rate for men at more than twice the rate for women. In England and Wales in 2023, about three in every four people who died by suicide were men, and the highest rate was among men in their late forties. Women more often report suicidal thoughts and attempts; men more often die.

Earlier chapters described why men can be hard to read in distress. Many have learned to show it as irritability, busyness or drinking rather than sadness, and to say “I'm fine” when they are not. In a study of young survivors of nearly lethal attempts, Thomas Simon and colleagues found that being male, getting into fights and feeling hopeless distinguished those who had acted impulsively. Anger and recklessness can be part of the picture, not a sign that someone is coping.

One influential account of why people come to want to die is the interpersonal theory, set out by Thomas Joiner and developed by Kimberly Van Orden and colleagues in 2010. It proposes that the wish to die grows most dangerous when two feelings meet: that one does not belong, and that one is a burden on others. The evidence is mixed, with the burden idea best supported, and critics argue that the theory leaves out culture and circumstance. But it points to two things a friend can affect. You can include someone, so that belonging is felt rather than assumed. And you can let them help you, ask their advice and tell them they matter, which answers the belief that they are only a weight.

The figure here sits alone with a phone, connected to everyone and to no one. Belonging is not the same as being near people. It is being expected, and being noticed when you do not turn up.
teach.disconfirm: The figures would be wrong for any country where men die by suicide at similar or lower rates than women; there are such places, which is why the numbers here are given by place and year. The interpersonal theory would be weakened if burden and belonging failed to predict the wish to die, and some studies find only weak links.

teach.p:
If what you see and hear worries you, ask. Ask directly, using the word: “Are you thinking about suicide?” or “Are you thinking about killing yourself?” It feels brutal to write. Said gently, at a private moment, it is a kindness, because it tells the person that you can hear the answer.

Many people fear that asking will put the idea in someone's head. The research says otherwise. In 2014, Dazzi and colleagues reviewed thirteen studies that had asked people about suicide and measured the effect; none found a significant increase in suicidal thinking, and some suggested that it fell. A 2018 meta-analysis by Blades and colleagues, covering eighteen studies, reached the same conclusion: asking does not increase risk and may bring a small benefit. Many people who have been suicidal describe relief at being asked.

How you ask matters. Avoid questions that signal the answer you want, such as “You're not thinking of doing anything stupid, are you?”, which invite a no. Avoid vague phrases like “hurting yourself”, which can mean something else. Describe what you have noticed first, as specific behaviour, as earlier chapters taught: “You've been really quiet since the summer, and last week you said we'd be better off without you. I'm worried about you. Are you thinking about suicide?”

Choose the setting with care. Side by side, on a walk, in a car or on a bench, often works better for men than across a table, as the chapter on the “I'm fine” mask described. Give the answer time to come. If the answer is no and you are still worried, say that the door is open, and ask again another day. A no is not a failure. You have shown that this is something they can talk to you about.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if studies found that being asked about suicide increased suicidal thinking or behaviour. The reviews by Dazzi and by Blades found no increase, though most studies measured thoughts rather than deaths, which are rare.
teach.pullQuote: Asking does not plant the idea. It tells the person you can hear the answer.

teach.h: If the answer is yes: stay, listen, and judge the urgency.
teach.p:
If the answer is yes, your body will react. Your breath may catch and your stomach drop. That is normal. Breathe out, stay where you are, and say something simple: “Thank you for telling me. I'm glad you did.” You do not need the right words. You need to stay.

Then listen. Let them tell you what has been happening, without arguing, lecturing or rushing to fix it. Do not tell them how much they have to live for or how upset other people would be; it usually feels like being told that their pain is wrong. Reflect what you hear: “It sounds like you've been carrying this on your own for a long time.” As the chapter on the mask described, listening matters more than solving.

You also need to know how urgent things are. It is reasonable to ask whether they have thought about how or when, and whether they have the means. You do not need the details; the answers tell you how much danger they are in now. If they have a plan and the means, or you believe they are in immediate danger, do not leave them alone. Call the emergency services, or a crisis line, with them. If they are not in immediate danger, agree on the next step together, such as calling a crisis line now or seeing a doctor tomorrow, and if you can, make sure they do not go home to an empty evening.

Do not promise to keep it secret. You can say: “I care about you too much to keep this to myself, but we'll decide together who we tell and how.” Most people accept this, and it keeps you honest. You are not their therapist. Your job is to stay with them and help them reach people who can help.
teach.disconfirm: This advice would be wrong if staying and listening made things worse; crisis services such as the 988 Lifeline recommend exactly these steps. Your judgment of urgency will be rough, so when in doubt, treat it as urgent.

teach.h: Time, distance and a written plan.
teach.p:
Many suicidal crises are short. In a study of people aged thirteen to thirty-four who had survived nearly lethal attempts, Simon and colleagues found that about one in four had spent less than five minutes between deciding to act and acting. The urge can be intense, and it can pass. Anything that puts time and distance between a person in crisis and a way to end their life gives the crisis room to pass.

This is called means safety. With the person's agreement, it can mean asking a trusted friend to keep a firearm for a while, keeping medicines locked away or in small amounts, or removing anything else the person has thought of using. It is not a sign of distrust; it is like taking a friend's car keys when they have been drinking. And getting through the crisis matters, because most people who survive a suicide attempt do not later die by suicide. In a review of ninety studies of people treated in hospital after self-harm, Owens and colleagues found that after nine years about seven in a hundred had died by suicide. That is a serious risk, and it also means that most lived.

A safety plan helps here. Developed by Barbara Stanley and Gregory Brown, it is a short written list, usually made with a clinician or crisis worker, of what to do as a crisis builds: the person's own warning signs, things they can do alone to get through, people and places that distract, people to ask for help, professional and crisis contacts, and ways to make the surroundings safer. In 2018, Stanley and colleagues compared about twelve hundred patients in veterans' emergency departments who received safety planning and follow-up calls with patients at sites that offered usual care. Those who received it had 45 per cent fewer suicidal behaviours over six months, and more than twice the odds of attending treatment. It was not a randomised trial, but the result is encouraging. You can help someone keep their plan where they will find it, and be one of the names on it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if removing access simply moved people to other means without reducing deaths; studies of means restriction mostly find that total deaths fall. The safety-planning result came from a comparison of sites rather than a randomised trial, and could partly reflect differences between them.

teach.h: Follow up, and look after yourself.
teach.p:
The days and weeks after a crisis matter as much as the conversation. In 2001, Jerome Motto and Alan Bostrom reported a trial with 843 people who had been admitted to hospital with depression or suicidal thoughts and had then refused further treatment. Some were sent short, caring letters, twenty-four over five years, asking nothing except that they knew someone was thinking of them. The group who received letters had lower suicide rates during the years the letters came, a difference that was statistically significant in the first two years. Later trials of caring contacts have had mixed results, but the idea has spread because it is cheap, kind and plausible.

You can do the same. Send a message the next day, and the week after, and the month after that. Keep it short and ask for nothing: “Thinking of you. Pint on Thursday?” Mark the anniversaries and the hard dates. Keep inviting them, even when they say no.

Then look after yourself. Hearing that someone you care about wants to die is frightening, and many people carry it alone afterwards, replaying the conversation. Talk to someone you trust, sharing no more than you need to. Crisis lines also support people who are worried about someone else. You are not responsible for another person's life on your own, and you cannot watch over anyone every hour. What you can do is ask, stay, connect and follow up.

And if someone you know dies by suicide, despite everyone's care, the grief that follows is often tangled with guilt and unanswerable questions. It is not proof that you failed them. Support groups exist specifically for people bereaved by suicide, and everything in the chapter on grief applies to you, with extra gentleness.
teach.disconfirm: Caring contacts would be called into doubt if well-run trials consistently found no benefit. Later trials have been mixed, so treat follow-up as a sensible kindness with promising evidence rather than a proven cure.

poseGallery.doCaption: Side by side, on a bench or a walk
poseGallery.dontCaption: Across a table, like an interview
poseGallery.annotation: Hard questions are easier to answer when neither person has to hold eye contact. Sitting side by side lowers the stakes for both of you.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Half listening, an eye on the time
poseGallery.annotation: After a yes, unhurried attention is the most useful thing you can give. If time really is short, say so and agree when you will come back, rather than glancing away.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Turning away when the answer is yes
poseGallery.annotation: Shock is normal, and the body shows it. Breathe out, turn back and stay in the conversation, because the person is watching how you take it.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Handing over a number and leaving
poseGallery.annotation: A number written on a card is easy to put away. Offering to sit with someone while they call, or to call together, turns a suggestion into a connection.

poseGallery.doCaption: Asking him plainly, and staying to listen
poseGallery.dontCaption: Hearing "I'm ready to go" and changing the subject
poseGallery.annotation: Talk of having had enough can sound like the realism of age. Treat it as a reason to ask directly, and to stay for the answer.

poseGallery.doCaption: A lift home, and the question asked in the car
poseGallery.dontCaption: Laughing off "they'd be better off without me"
poseGallery.annotation: A dark remark that makes the room go quiet deserves a private follow-up. Side by side, ask plainly whether he is thinking about suicide.

caseStudy:
Sam, forty-four, has played five-a-side football with Dev, forty-six, every Tuesday for eight years. Over the winter, after Dev's business folds and he moves out of the family home, Sam notices changes. Dev misses two games, then comes back thinner and unshaven. He picks a fight with a younger player over nothing. In the pub afterwards he drinks fast and says little. One evening, when someone jokes about money, Dev says flatly that his kids would be better off without him, and laughs. Nobody else seems to notice.

Sam does. He remembers the word burden from a training day at work, and he knows he cannot tell from Dev's face what Dev means. The next Tuesday he offers Dev a lift home and, parked outside the flat with the engine off, says: “Mate, you've not been yourself since Christmas, and what you said last week about the kids has stuck with me. I'm worried. Are you thinking about suicide?”

Dev stares straight ahead for a long time. Then he says yes, most nights. Sam's stomach turns over. He breathes out and says, “Thank you for telling me.” He listens for nearly an hour. He asks whether Dev is in danger tonight; Dev says he does not think so, but that the evenings are the worst. Sam asks if they can call a crisis line together now, and Dev agrees, on speaker, in the car. The counsellor helps them make a plan: Dev will see his doctor in the morning, Sam will drive him, and Dev's brother will stay with him for a few days and look after anything in the flat that worries him.

The doctor refers Dev for treatment. Sam texts him every few days, nothing heavy. Dev comes back to Tuesdays in the spring. Months later, he tells Sam that the question in the car was the first time anyone had asked, and that he had been waiting for someone to.
observe: Notice how people around you talk about suicide, including phrases like “committed suicide” and jokes. The language people hear shapes whether they believe they can speak.
Notice who in your life has gone quiet, stopped turning up or changed over the past few months. You do not need to act on everything; notice, and consider a check-in.
Notice your own body's reaction when you read or hear the word suicide. That reaction is what you will need to breathe through when you ask.
Notice the side-by-side moments in your week, such as drives, walks or shared jobs, in which a hard question could be asked.

drills.name: Say the Words
steps: Write down the direct question, in the words you would use: “Are you thinking about suicide?”
Say it aloud, alone, ten times, until your voice is steady.
Write the sentence you would use before it, describing what you had noticed.
Say both sentences aloud together, slowly and gently.
If you have a willing friend who knows the purpose, practise once with them, then swap roles.
variations: Practise saying the sentence you would use after the question if the answer were no, so that you can keep the door open.
Write the question in words that fit a particular person in your life, and say it aloud as if to them.

drills.name: Your Region's Line
steps: Open the crisis resources in this app and find the line for where you live.
Save the number in your phone under a name you will recognise in a hurry.
Write down your local emergency number and how to reach a doctor out of hours.
Write the first sentence you would say if you called about someone else.
Check that the people closest to you know these numbers too.
variations: Find the crisis line for a country where someone you love lives, and save it too.
Show one person close to you where the crisis resources are in this app, and ask them to save the number.

drills.name: A Plan for Yourself First
steps: On a calm day, write down your own early signs of a very bad patch: thoughts, feelings, behaviour.
Write three things you can do alone that help you get through a hard evening.
Write the people and places that take your mind off things, and the people you could ask for help.
Add the professional and crisis numbers you found in the previous drill.
Write one thing that would make your surroundings safer on a bad night, and keep the page where you will find it.
variations: Show your plan to one person you trust, and ask whether they would be willing to be one of the names on it.
Review your plan in three months, and update anything that has changed, such as numbers or people.

drills.name: The First Five Minutes
steps: Write what you would say first if someone answered yes.
Write two listening sentences that reflect what you hear, without fixing.
Write how you would ask about urgency, and the answers that would mean calling emergency services.
Write how you would explain that you cannot keep it secret.
Write how you would help them connect, and who you would talk to afterwards.
variations: Practise the first five minutes aloud with a willing friend, taking turns, and stop at once if either of you finds it too much.
Write down what you would say to a crisis line if you called about someone who was with you.

drills.name: The Follow-Up Habit
steps: List three people in your life who have had a hard year.
For each, write a short message that asks for nothing in return.
Set reminders in your phone to check in with each over the next two months.
Send the first message this week.
Note how each person responds, without needing a reply.
variations: Add a reminder for an anniversary or hard date for one of the people on your list.
Write one message you could send to someone you have lost touch with who had a hard year.

quiz.q: Does asking someone directly whether they are thinking about suicide make suicide more likely?
options: Yes, because the question itself can put the idea into a person's head
Only if you use the word suicide instead of a gentler phrase
No; reviews find that asking does not increase suicidal thinking
It depends mainly on whether the person asked is a man or woman
quiz.explain: Reviews by Dazzi and colleagues and by Blades and colleagues found no increase in suicidal thinking after people were asked, and some found small benefits. Using the word clearly is recommended, because vague phrases can be misread.

quiz.q: What did Franklin and colleagues' 2017 review of fifty years of research find about predicting suicide?
options: Known risk factors predicted it only slightly better than chance
Trained clinicians could predict it accurately from body language
Depression alone predicted almost every suicide in later life
Prediction had improved steadily with each decade of new studies
quiz.explain: Across 365 studies, risk factors predicted suicidal thoughts and behaviour only slightly better than chance, and prediction had not improved over time. This is why the body, or any single sign, should prompt a question rather than a conclusion.

quiz.q: A friend who has been withdrawn for weeks says, half joking, “Everyone would be better off without me.” What is the best next step?
options: Tell him firmly that it is not true, and then change the subject
Find a private moment, ask him directly about suicide, and listen
Make a joke to lighten the mood, and then check in next month
Wait to see whether his body language shows any clearer signs
quiz.explain: Talking about being a burden is one of the clearest warning signs, even when it is said as a joke. Waiting for the body to confirm it is a mistake, because the body cannot; asking directly, in private, is the next step.

quiz.q: Why does putting time and distance between a person in crisis and dangerous means help?
options: It forces the person to rely on willpower until the feeling goes
It means that the person no longer needs professional help at all
It shows the person that the people around them do not trust them
Many suicidal crises are brief, and the urge can pass if delayed
quiz.explain: In Simon and colleagues' study, about one in four survivors of nearly lethal attempts had spent less than five minutes between deciding and acting. Delay gives the crisis room to pass, and it works alongside professional help, not instead of it.

quiz.q: You ask a colleague, and she says yes, she has been thinking about ending her life, and asks you to keep it secret. What should you do?
options: Thank her, stay with her, and explain you'll help her get support
Promise to keep the secret so that she goes on trusting you in future
Go straight to her manager without saying anything more to her
Give her the helpline number and leave her to make the call alone
quiz.explain: Promising secrecy can leave you holding a danger alone, and going behind her back breaks trust. Thank her, stay, judge the urgency, and decide together who to tell and how, helping her make the call rather than leaving her with a number.

quiz.q: In Motto and Bostrom's trial, what did some people who had refused further care receive, and what happened?
options: Daily phone calls from a psychiatrist, and nobody in the group died
A single long letter, which had no measurable effect at any point
Short, regular caring letters; suicide rates were lower while they came
Weekly home visits, after which rates fell only once visits stopped
quiz.explain: The contact group received twenty-four short letters over five years that asked for nothing. Their suicide rates were lower during the years of contact, significantly so in the first two years, which is why brief, regular follow-up is recommended.

quiz.q: What did Stanley and colleagues find for patients in veterans' emergency departments who received safety planning and follow-up calls?
options: Fewer suicidal behaviours over six months, and better attendance at treatment
No difference at all compared with the patients who received usual care at other sites
More suicidal behaviour, because writing down a plan made people think about suicide
Better results only for patients who had never been to an emergency department before
quiz.explain: Patients who received safety planning and follow-up calls had 45 per cent fewer suicidal behaviours over six months and more than twice the odds of attending treatment. It was not a randomised trial, but the result is encouraging.

quiz.q: Late at night, your brother, who has been low for weeks, texts "Sorry for everything. Love you." What fits this chapter best?
options: Reply in the morning, since he is probably just tired and feeling sorry for himself
Text back telling him not to be silly and that everything will look better tomorrow
Call him now, ask directly about suicide, and get help if he is in danger
Post on his social media asking his friends whether anyone knows what is going on
quiz.explain: A goodbye-like message after weeks of low mood is a warning sign that calls for action now. Ring, ask plainly, judge the urgency, and if he is in danger, stay with him while someone calls the emergency services.

quiz.q: Someone says that people who talk about suicide are just seeking attention and do not mean it. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since people who really mean it never talk about it beforehand
Talk of suicide should be taken seriously every time and followed up
It is right for young people, though older people's talk should be taken seriously
It is right, so the kindest response is to ignore it and not encourage them
quiz.explain: Talking about wanting to die is one of the clearest warning signs, and crisis services advise taking it seriously every time, however it is said. Someone seeking attention by talking about suicide needs attention.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person in your life whom you would want to ask, if you were ever worried about them, or think of a time when you were worried about someone and did not ask. What did you notice, and what stopped you? Write the exact words you would use now, starting with what you had noticed and ending with the direct question. Then write what you would say first if the answer were yes, and where you would sit or walk while you asked.
reflection.guidance: Write the words exactly, because the question is easier to say once it has been written down. If you did not ask someone in the past and things went badly, be gentle with yourself; most people were never taught how. If this chapter has stirred thoughts of suicide in you, please use the resources at the start of the chapter now, or talk to someone you trust today.

failureMode: The most dangerous failure is to wait for the body to tell you: to assume that someone is safe because they still go to work, still laugh or do not look low enough, when no posture or face can show whether a person is thinking about suicide. The second is not to ask, out of fear of planting the idea, which the research does not support, or to ask in a way that invites a no. The third is to meet a yes by arguing, lecturing, promising secrecy or leaving the person alone. The fourth is to forget time and distance: a crisis can pass when dangerous means are out of reach and a plan is in place. The fifth is to stop after one conversation, when following up is part of the help. And the last is to carry it all yourself. Ask, stay, connect, follow up, and get support for yourself too.

furtherStudy.author: Thomas Joiner
furtherStudy.note: Harvard University Press, 2005. The interpersonal theory, written for general readers by a psychologist whose own father died by suicide.

furtherStudy.author: T. Dazzi, R. Gribble, S. Wessely and N. T. Fear
furtherStudy.note: Psychological Medicine 44(16), 2014. The review behind the advice to ask directly.

furtherStudy.work: Safety Planning Intervention: A brief intervention to mitigate suicide risk
furtherStudy.author: Barbara Stanley and Gregory K. Brown
furtherStudy.note: Cognitive and Behavioral Practice 19(2), 2012. The safety plan, step by step, from its developers.

furtherStudy.work: Preventing suicide: a resource for media professionals
furtherStudy.author: World Health Organization and International Association for Suicide Prevention

moreCases.title: The goodbye email
moreCases.scene:
Priya manages a team of twelve at an engineering consultancy. On a Thursday evening she receives an email from Martin, fifty, one of her
  most experienced engineers, sent to the whole team. It thanks everyone for the years they have worked together, says how much he has valued
  each of them, and mentions by name the people he wants to have his books and the plant on his desk. It ends, "Look after each other." Martin
  has not resigned. He is not due any leave.

  Two of the team reply with cheerful messages, assuming he must have a new job he has not told them about. One jokes that she will fight anyone for
  the plant.

  Priya reads the email twice. She knows that Martin's wife left him in the spring, that he has been quiet and thin for months, and that last week,
  when someone mentioned the pension scheme, he said he would not need to worry about that.

Priya also remembers that Martin had asked her, a fortnight ago, whether his life insurance through work was still valid, which had seemed an odd question at the time and which she had answered without thinking about it.

It is nearly eight in the evening. The office is empty, and Priya is on the train home. She knows that Martin lives alone now, in a flat across the city, and that nobody in the team has his family's numbers.
moreCases.misread:
The team read the email as a farewell before a new job, because that is the usual reason for a message thanking colleagues and giving things away. Nobody connected it with the months of change in Martin or with his remark about the pension.

The joke about the plant also showed how easily a group follows the most comfortable reading. Once two people had treated the email as cheerful, it became harder for anyone else to say it frightened them.
moreCases.betterRead: Saying goodbye as though for the last time, and giving away things that matter, are among the warning signs that crisis services list, and together with months of withdrawal and a comment that hinted at no future, they made a pattern that called for action that evening, not on Monday. A reader cannot know from an email what someone intends. Priya did not need to know. She rang Martin straight away. When he answered, she said, "Martin, I got your email, and I'm worried about you. Are you thinking about suicide?" After a long silence he said yes. Priya thanked him for telling her, stayed on the phone and asked whether he was safe right now. He said he was not sure. She asked whether she could call the emergency services to his address while she stayed on the line with him, and he agreed. She kept talking to him until they arrived. He was looked after in hospital that night, and over the following weeks a crisis team supported him at home. Priya visited, and kept in touch. In the autumn, Martin came back to work, and he still has the plant.

moreCases.title: The son who said 'what's the point'
moreCases.scene:
Carl's son, Ethan, sixteen, has been struggling since his exam results in August were worse than he hoped and his girlfriend ended their
  relationship. He spends most of his time in his room, has stopped going to football, and barely eats with the family. Carl has put it down to
  being sixteen. Then, one evening, Ethan's younger sister shows Carl a message Ethan posted on a group chat with his friends: "Honestly what's
  the point of any of it. Won't be around to see it anyway." One friend has replied with a laughing face.

  Carl's wife wants to confiscate Ethan's phone and ground him for posting something so upsetting. Carl's instinct is to say nothing, in case
  asking makes things worse.

  Carl remembers a leaflet from Ethan's school about talking to teenagers, and the advice that asking directly is safe.

Carl has also noticed that Ethan has stopped gaming with his friends online, which used to take up most of his evenings, and that his light is often on at three in the morning when Carl gets up for the toilet.

Carl has also noticed that Ethan has deleted most of his photos from the past year, and that last week he gave his younger sister his favourite hoodie, the one he has worn almost every day since he was fourteen, saying he did not need it any more. Carl had thought it was a kind gesture between siblings, and had said so.
moreCases.misread:
Carl's wife read the message as bad behaviour to be punished, and Carl's own first reading was that the safest thing was not to ask, for fear of putting the idea in Ethan's head. Both readings would have left Ethan alone with what he had written.

The friend's laughing reply also mattered. It told Ethan that the message had landed as a joke, which may have been what he hoped, and may have been what he feared.
moreCases.betterRead: Talk of having no future, even in a group chat and even with a laughing reply beneath it, is one of the clearest warning signs, and it should be taken seriously every time. The research is clear that asking directly does not increase risk: Dazzi and colleagues and Blades and colleagues found no increase in suicidal thinking from being asked, and some evidence that it helped. Carl knocked on Ethan's door that evening, sat on the end of the bed, and said, "I saw what you put on the group chat. I'm not angry. I'm worried about you. Are you thinking about suicide?" Ethan was silent, then said sometimes, at night, but not tonight. Carl listened. He did not argue or tell Ethan how much he had to live for. He asked whether they could see the doctor together the next day, and whether Ethan would be all right with him telling Ethan's mum. Ethan agreed to both. The doctor referred him to the young people's mental health service, and the school was told, with Ethan's permission. Carl checked in every evening, briefly, and in the spring Ethan went back to football.

moreCases.title: The widower who was 'ready to go'
moreCases.scene:
Alan, seventy-nine, lost his wife, Joan, eighteen months ago after fifty-four years of marriage. His daughter, Linda, visits every Sunday.
  Over the winter she notices that he has stopped going to his bowls club, that he has given his golf clubs to his grandson, and that he has
  started saying things like "I've had a good innings" and "I'm ready to go now, love, I've had my life." He says them cheerfully, while making
  the tea.

  Linda's husband tells her that this is what old people say, and that her father is simply being realistic about his age. Linda half agrees.
  Her father has never been a man for drama, and he does not seem unhappy, exactly. He seems settled.

  But she also notices that he has written out a list of where all his papers are and left it on the kitchen table, where she would see it, and
  that he has asked her twice whether she would look after Joan's cat.

Linda also remembers that her mother's death was sudden, a stroke in the kitchen, and that her father found her. He has never talked about that morning, and Linda has never asked.

When Linda mentions the list of papers, her father laughs and says that someone has to be organised in this family. She laughs too, and then feels sick on the drive home.
moreCases.misread:
Linda's husband read Alan's remarks as the ordinary realism of old age, and his calm as acceptance. Older men's talk about being ready to go is often treated this way, and it is one reason their distress can be overlooked.

His cheerfulness also made the remarks easier to dismiss. People expect distress to sound distressed, and Alan's lightness hid how far his thinking had gone.
moreCases.betterRead: Older men, especially after bereavement, are among the people whose warning signs are most easily missed, because talk of having had enough can sound like ordinary acceptance of age. Alan's cluster went beyond that: withdrawing from his club, giving away things that mattered, putting his affairs in order and asking about the cat, alongside repeated talk of being ready to go. The chapter notes that a sudden calm can mean many things, and that it is a reason to check in. Linda asked, the following Sunday, side by side on the bench in his garden: "Dad, you've given away your clubs and written out where everything is, and you keep saying you're ready to go. I'm worried about you. Are you thinking about ending your life?" Alan was quiet for a while, then said that he thought about it, because he did not see what he was for any more. Linda listened, then told him how much he still mattered to them all. She asked him to come with her to his doctor, and he agreed. The doctor arranged support; Linda found a widowers' bereavement group that met on Thursdays. Alan went, grumbling, and went back the next week.

moreCases.title: The friend who said no
moreCases.scene:
Hamid and Leo have been friends since university. Leo, thirty-three, was made redundant in the summer and has been low ever since: he has
  stopped answering messages for days at a time, and when they meet he drinks more than he used to and says very little. One night, over a
  takeaway, Leo says that he feels like he has failed at everything, and that his family would be better off if they did not have to worry about
  him.

  Hamid takes a breath and asks him directly whether he is thinking about suicide. Leo looks surprised, then says no, he is not, he is just fed up,
  and he did not mean it like that.

  Hamid is not sure whether to believe him. He feels awkward, and worries that he has made things weird between them.

Hamid has done a short mental health awareness course through work, and the trainer said that the worst thing you can do is not ask. He did not expect to need it so soon, or to feel so awkward when he did.

Leo has also stopped going to the gym, which he used to go to five times a week, and has started sleeping until the afternoon. His flat, which he used to keep spotless, is full of takeaway boxes, and he has not opened his post for weeks.
moreCases.misread:
Hamid's worry was that a no meant he had misread the situation and made things worse by asking. He also wondered whether he should keep pressing until Leo admitted something.

And Hamid's awkwardness was not a sign that he had done something wrong. It was simply what asking a hard question feels like the first time.

Leo's own surprise also mattered. People often deny thoughts the first time they are asked, because the question catches them off guard, and then come back to it later once they know it is safe.
moreCases.betterRead: A no is not a failure. Asking showed Leo that suicide was something he could talk to Hamid about, and that is valuable whatever the answer is on the night. Pressing past a no tends to feel like an accusation. The better response, which Hamid managed, was to accept the answer, keep the door open, and stay in touch: "OK. I'm glad. But if that ever changes, or if things get that bad, I want you to tell me. Any time." He then asked about the job search and offered to look over Leo's CV. Over the next two months he messaged every few days, asking nothing heavy, and they kept meeting. In November, Leo rang him late one evening and said that things had got worse and that he had started thinking about it, and that he was ringing because Hamid had told him to. Hamid stayed on the phone, they called a crisis line together, and Leo saw his doctor the next morning. Later, Leo told him that the question in the summer, and the fact that Hamid had not made a big deal of the no, was why he had known who to call.

workedReading.title: The message at midnight
workedReading.scene:
Rachel, thirty-eight, is getting ready for bed when her phone buzzes. It is her younger brother, Tom, thirty-four, who has been struggling since his divorce and his move to a city three hours away. The message says: "Sorry for everything. I love you. Tell Mum I'm sorry." Tom does not usually text late, and he never says he loves her. Over the past few weeks his messages have been short and flat, and on the phone at the weekend he said he did not see things getting better.

Rachel and Tom have always been close, but since the divorce he has been harder to reach. She had been meaning to visit for weeks and had kept putting it off.

Rachel also knows that their father died when Tom was twelve, and that Tom has always found it hardest of all of them to ask for help. She has never heard him sound the way he sounded at the weekend.

steps.label: Take it seriously
steps.text:
Rachel's first thought is that she might be overreacting. Her second is that this message, after weeks of low, flat contact and talk of nothing getting better, has the shape of a goodbye. She decides that she would rather be wrong and embarrassed than not act, and that the next step is to reach him now, not in the morning.

She also notes that the message mentions their mother, and an apology to her. Messages that try to settle things with the people closest to someone are among the goodbyes that crisis services describe.

steps.label: Reach him, and ask plainly
steps.text:
She rings him immediately. He answers on the fifth ring, quietly. She says, "Tom, I've just seen your message, and I'm really worried about you. Are you thinking about suicide?" There is a long pause, and then he says yes. Rachel's stomach drops. She breathes out and says, "Thank you for telling me. I'm so glad you picked up."

She also keeps her voice low and steady, even though her heart is racing. The person at the other end is listening to how she sounds as much as to what she says.

steps.label: Judge how urgent it is
steps.text:
She asks, gently, whether he is safe right now, tonight. He says he does not know. She asks whether he has thought about how, and he says yes. She does not ask for any details. The answers tell her that he is in danger now, and that this is not a conversation to finish and pick up tomorrow.

She also resists the urge to ask why, or to tell him he cannot do this. Those questions can wait. What matters now is whether he is safe and how to keep him that way.

steps.label: Get help while you stay
steps.text:
Rachel keeps Tom on the phone and signals to her partner, Dan, to call the emergency services for Tom's address from his own phone. She tells Tom that she is not going anywhere, and asks him to stay on the line with her. She asks whether there is anyone nearby who could come round, and whether he would move to a different room from where he is. She talks to him about ordinary things: his dog, their mum, the holiday they went on as children. She listens far more than she speaks.

She also keeps her questions simple and gives him small things to do: stay on the line, sit down, tell her about the dog. Small, concrete requests are easier to follow in a crisis than big ones.

steps.label: Be honest about telling
steps.text:
When Tom asks her not to tell anyone, she says, "I love you too much to keep this to myself. Dan's calling someone who can help tonight, and tomorrow we'll decide together who else needs to know." Tom is quiet, then says OK. Rachel stays on the phone until she hears a knock at his door and voices she does not know, and then she speaks to the paramedics herself.

She also tells him what will happen next, so that the knock on the door does not come as a shock: someone is coming to help, they will be kind, and she will stay on the phone until they arrive.

steps.label: Follow up
steps.text:
Tom is taken to hospital, assessed and supported by a crisis team over the following weeks. Rachel drives up the next day and stays for the weekend. She helps him make a safety plan with the crisis worker, and her name and number go on it. After she goes home, she texts every day for a fortnight, and then every few days, never asking for much: a photo of his dog, a question about football. She puts the date of the midnight message in her calendar, so that she can check in on him next year.

She also asks the crisis worker, with Tom's agreement, what she should look out for and who she should ring if she is worried again, so that she is not left guessing.

steps.label: Look after yourself
steps.text:
For several weeks afterwards, Rachel cannot stop replaying the call. She talks to Dan and to a close friend, and rings a crisis line herself one evening, as someone worried about a family member, and finds it helps. She notes that she did not save Tom on her own. She asked, she stayed, she connected him to people who could help, and she kept in touch. In the spring, Tom tells her that he is still here because she rang straight back.

She also takes a few days off work, which she has never done for her own sake, and is surprised by how much she needs them.

moreFailures.title: Treating it as a joke or a bid for attention
moreFailures.body:
Talk of suicide is often said lightly: as a joke in the pub, a throwaway line in a group chat, a dark remark about money or a relationship. It is also often dismissed as attention-seeking. Both readings are dangerous. Crisis services are clear that talk about wanting to die, about being a burden or about having no future should be taken seriously every time, however it is said. If someone is seeking attention by talking about suicide, they need attention. The cost of a private, kind follow-up to a remark that turns out to mean nothing is a moment of awkwardness. The cost of ignoring one that meant everything cannot be undone.

It also helps to remember that people sometimes test the water with a light remark, to see how it lands. A friend who takes it seriously, gently and privately, may be the first person who has.

And remember that someone who has talked about suicide before and not acted is not safe for that reason. Every time is worth taking seriously.

moreFailures.title: Asking in a way that invites a no
moreFailures.body:
"You're not thinking of doing anything silly, are you?" "You wouldn't do anything stupid, would you?" Questions like these are asked out of fear and love, and they tell the person which answer you want to hear. Most people give it. They also carry a judgment, that the thought is silly or stupid, which adds shame to whatever the person is carrying. Ask plainly, using the word, and in a tone that says you can hear either answer: "Are you thinking about suicide?" Describe what you have noticed first, so that the question has a reason. And then wait, for as long as the answer takes.

It also helps to avoid euphemisms of your own, such as "ending it" or "doing something". They can be misunderstood, and they can suggest that you cannot bring yourself to say the word, which makes it harder for the other person to say it too.

moreFailures.title: Arguing them out of it
moreFailures.body:
When someone says yes, many people's instinct is to argue: you have so much to live for, think of your children, things are not that bad, other people have it worse. It comes from love and panic, and it usually lands as a sign that you have not understood how much pain they are in, or that their pain is wrong. It can end the conversation. Listen instead. Reflect back what you hear. Ask what has been happening. Reasons to live matter, and they often come out in the conversation, but they are far more powerful when the person finds them than when you list them.

It also helps to resist minimising: "It's not that bad" or "You'll feel better tomorrow". However the situation looks from outside, it feels unbearable from inside, and being told otherwise can make someone feel more alone.

moreFailures.title: Keeping it secret, or carrying it alone
moreFailures.body:
Someone who tells you they are thinking about suicide may ask you to keep it secret, and promising feels like the way to keep their trust. It is a promise you cannot safely keep. Say instead that you care too much to keep it to yourself, and that you will decide together who to tell and how. Then help them connect to people who can help: a crisis line, their doctor, a family member. Carrying it alone is also a risk for you. Talk to someone you trust, and use the crisis lines yourself if you need to, because they support people who are worried about someone as well as people who are struggling.

It also helps to know in advance who you would tell. If someone you care about says yes, it is far easier to act quickly if you already know their doctor, their family or the crisis line for where they live.

And if the person later thanks you, or does not, either is fine. You did not do it to be thanked.

questions.q: What if they get angry with me for asking?
questions.a:
Some people do react with anger or embarrassment at first, especially if they are not ready to talk or if they feel caught out. It does not mean you were wrong to ask. Stay calm, and say why you asked: "I asked because I care about you, and because I've been worried." Do not argue or press. Leave the door open: "If you ever do want to talk, about anything, I'm here." And keep in touch afterwards, as usual, so that the question does not become a wall between you. Many people who were angry at being asked say later that it mattered that someone did.

It may also help to remember that the question has done its work even if they are angry. They now know that you noticed, that you care, and that suicide is something they could raise with you.

questions.q: What can I do if they live far away?
questions.a:
A great deal. Call rather than text, so that you can hear them and they can hear you. Ask directly. If they say they are in danger now, stay on the line and ask someone else to call the emergency services for their address, or call them yourself and give the address; emergency services can be reached for someone in another area. If they are not in immediate danger, help them connect with local help, such as a crisis line or their doctor, and ask whether there is someone nearby who could be with them. Then keep in touch: regular calls and messages from a distance still help someone feel that they belong.

It also helps to know the emergency number in the country where they live, if it is different from yours, and to save it in your phone alongside their address.

questions.q: What if I say the wrong thing?
questions.a:
There are no perfect words, and you do not need them. What matters most is that you ask, use the word, listen without arguing, and stay. If you say something clumsy, you can say so: "That came out wrong. What I mean is that I care about you and I'm worried." People who have been suicidal often say that it was not the words that helped but the fact that someone noticed, asked and did not run away. If you freeze, a simple "I'm here" and a few minutes of quiet company are far better than a perfect sentence never said.

It also helps to remember that you are not trying to talk them out of anything. You are trying to stay with them long enough for help to arrive, and to let them know they are not alone.

It may also help to practise. The first drill in this chapter asks you to say the question aloud until your voice is steady, and many people find that a few minutes of practice make the real moment much less frightening.

questions.q: Should I mention it if I see something worrying online?
questions.a:
Yes. A post, a message or a status that talks about wanting to die, having no future or saying goodbye is a warning sign, just as it would be in person, as Carl found with Ethan's group chat. Reach out privately, by phone if you can, rather than replying in public. Ask directly how they are and whether they are thinking about suicide. If you believe someone is in immediate danger and you cannot reach them, contact the emergency services. Most social media platforms also have ways to report posts about self-harm or suicide so that support can be offered.

It also helps to keep the conversation private. Replying publicly can embarrass the person, invite comments that make things worse, and turn a moment of honesty into a spectacle.

If you see something worrying and you do not know the person well, you can still reach out kindly, or let someone closer to them know what you saw, so that it is not left unanswered.

questions.q: How can I support someone bereaved by suicide?
questions.a:
Gently, and for a long time. Grief after suicide is often tangled with guilt, anger, shame and questions that have no answer, and many bereaved people feel isolated, because others do not know what to say and stay away. Say the name of the person who died. Do not ask how it happened, or speculate about why. Do not suggest that anyone could have prevented it. Offer practical help, as the chapter on grief describes, and keep offering it for months. Support groups exist specifically for people bereaved by suicide, and many find them helpful because everyone there understands. People bereaved by suicide can themselves be at higher risk, so keep in touch, and ask how they are.

It also helps to look after yourself if you were close to the person who died. Many people bereaved by suicide find that the grief comes in waves for years, and that support, from friends, groups or professionals, helps.

questions.q: What if I am the one thinking about suicide?
questions.a:
Please tell someone now. You do not have to manage these thoughts on your own, and they do not mean that you will act on them. The crisis lines listed at the start of this chapter are free, confidential and open now, by phone or text in many countries. If you are in danger, call the emergency services. If you can, tell someone you trust, and see your doctor. Many people who have felt this way say that the feeling, however strong, changed with time and support. If you have made a safety plan, use it. If you have not, the third drill in this chapter can help you start one on a calmer day.

It may also help to know that asking for help is not a burden on the people who love you. Most would far rather know, and be able to help, than find out too late.

watch.title: Small Talk Saves Lives
watch.notice: A Samaritans campaign film on how a simple conversation can interrupt someone's suicidal thoughts. Notice how small the intervention is. If you are struggling yourself, the app's crisis resources are always available.

reviewPrompt: This week, save the crisis line for your region in your phone, and say the direct question aloud until you can say it gently and without hesitation.
